## Introduction

This tutorial covers [Chapter 6: Applications: Explore](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/explore-applications.html) from [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. You will learn the chapter's principles for communicating exploratory results: keep it simple, use color to draw attention, tell a story, put categories in a meaningful order, make labels easy to read, pick a purpose, and select meaningful colors.

### Exercise 1

You should be doing this tutorial in a repo named `applications-explore`. If you are not, create one and then connect to it.

Create a new file, `analysis.qmd`, with the title `"Applications: Explore"` and your name as the author. In a bash Terminal, render it:

```bash
quarto render analysis.qmd
```

Open `analysis.html` with Live Server (right-click it in the Explorer → **Open with Live Server**) and keep the tab open. It refreshes on every render. Going forward, we will just tell you to "Render" when we want you to take these steps.

Create a `.gitignore` with `analysis_files` followed by a blank line. Commit and push. Use AI however you like.

If `show_file()` fails, it is probably because you have not yet loaded `library(learnr2)` in the R Terminal.

```{r}
#| label: introduction-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file(".gitignore"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{.output}
analysis_files
```

###

This chapter focuses on how graphs can best be utilized to present data accurately and effectively. It has no new statistics, only better and worse ways to show the same numbers.

## Simplicity, color, and story

Graphs can powerfully communicate ideas directly and quickly. This section applies three principles, keep it simple, use color to draw attention, and tell a story, to a company's expenses and Duke University's monthly hires.

### Exercise 1

```{r}
#| label: simplicity-color-and-story-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question("In the bash Terminal, run cat data/expenses.csv. CP/CR.", type = "reflection")
```

###

```{.output}
category,percent
Cutting tools,3
Buildings and Administration,22
Labor,31
Machinery,27
Workplace materials,17
```

###

Consider a manufacturing company that has summarized its costs into five different categories. Each number is a percent of the company's total costs, and the five add up to 100.

### Exercise 2

Add a chunk that reads `data/expenses.csv` and prints it. Render.

```{r}
#| label: simplicity-color-and-story-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: simplicity-color-and-story-2-test
#| echo: true
read_csv("data/expenses.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

###

Labor, at 31%, is the biggest cost, and cutting tools, at 3%, the smallest. Buildings and Administration (22%) and Workplace materials (17%) differ by 5 percentage points.

### Exercise 3

Replace the printing so that the chunk draws a pie chart of `percent`, with one slice for each `category`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: simplicity-color-and-story-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: simplicity-color-and-story-3-test
#| echo: true
read_csv("data/expenses.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = "", y = percent, fill = category)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_polar(theta = "y")
```

###

Can your eye tell how different Buildings and Administration is from Workplace materials when looking at the slices of pie? The colors in the pie chart do not mean anything and are therefore distracting.

### Exercise 4

Replace the pie chart with a bar plot of the same numbers, with horizontal bars sorted from the largest cost to the smallest. Render.

```{r}
#| label: simplicity-color-and-story-4
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: simplicity-color-and-story-4-test
#| echo: true
read_csv("data/expenses.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = percent, y = fct_reorder(category, percent))) +
  geom_col()
```

###

The 5-point gap between Buildings and Administration and Workplace materials is now easy to see. Typically, a bar plot will be easier for the reader to digest than a pie chart, especially if the categorical data being plotted has more than just a few levels.

Give each bar its own color. Render.

```{r}
  ggplot(aes(x = percent, y = fct_reorder(category, percent), fill = category)) +
```

Colors can be distracting when they are only used to brighten up the plot. These five colors, and the legend that explains them, repeat what the y-axis already says.

### Exercise 6

Color the Buildings and Administration bar to draw attention to it, make the other four bars gray, and remove the legend. Render.


```{r}
#| label: simplicity-color-and-story-6-test
#| echo: true
read_csv("data/expenses.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = percent, y = fct_reorder(category, percent),
             fill = category == "Buildings and Administration")) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey70", "firebrick"))
```

###

An important principle to keep in mind is to use color to draw attention. The red bar is now the first thing a reader sees.

Hiring is flat at about 200 to 300 a month, jumps in June, peaks in July, and falls back by November. Nothing in the data says why.

### Exercise 10

Add a large point that marks July in a color that draws attention. Render.

```{r}
duke_hires |>
```

### Exercise 11

Add a vertical line at July and a text annotation beside it that explains the spike: July is the start of Duke's fiscal year. Render.

```{r}
#| label: simplicity-color-and-story-11
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: simplicity-color-and-story-11-test
#| echo: true
duke_hires <- read_csv("data/duke_hires_2010.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

duke_hires |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = hires)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 7, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = filter(duke_hires, month == 7),
             color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 7.3, y = 760, hjust = 0, size = 3.5,
           label = "Hires peak in July, which\nis the start of Duke's\nfiscal year.")
```

###

For many graphs, an important aspect is the inclusion of information which is not provided in the dataset that is being plotted. Your graph is now *annotated* with information about the start of the university's fiscal year, which contextualizes the information provided by the data.

### Exercise 12

Improve the plot. Label the months by name, start the y-axis at zero, and add a title, axis labels, a subtitle that states the main finding, and a caption giving the number of months and the source. Render.

```{r}
#| label: simplicity-color-and-story-12
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: simplicity-color-and-story-12-test
#| echo: true
duke_hires <- read_csv("data/duke_hires_2010.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

duke_hires |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = hires)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 7, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = filter(duke_hires, month == 7),
             color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 7.3, y = 760, hjust = 0, size = 3.5,
           label = "Hires peak in July, which\nis the start of Duke's\nfiscal year.") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = month.abb, minor_breaks = NULL) +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "Duke Hires by Month, 2010",
       subtitle = "July and August alone brought nearly a third of the year's 4,380 hires",
       x = NULL,
       y = "Hires",
       caption = "12 monthly counts; Duke University, via Introduction to Modern Statistics")
```

###

The book's annotation says hires always peak in July, but one year of data can only show that they peaked in 2010. The external information serves to contextualize the data and helps communicate the narrative of the research.

## Order, labels, purpose, and color

This section's four principles, order matters, make the labels easy to read, pick a purpose, and select meaningful colors, all use one poll about Brexit, Britain's exit from the European Union. Every plot shows the same 25 counts.

### Exercise 1

```{r}
#| label: order-labels-purpose-and-color-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question("In the bash Terminal, run head data/brexit.csv. CP/CR.", type = "reflection")
```

###

```{.output}
region,opinion,n
London,Very well,10
London,Fairly well,18
London,Fairly badly,33
London,Very badly,118
London,Don't know,16
Rest of South,Very well,49
Rest of South,Fairly well,93
Rest of South,Fairly badly,126
```

###

In September 2019, YouGov asked Great Britain adults, "How well or badly do you think the government are doing at handling Britain's exit from the European Union?" The five answers appear in each region in the order they were offered: Very well, Fairly well, Fairly badly, Very badly, and Don't know.


###

The Brexit survey results were broken down by region in Great Britain. Five regions times five answers makes 25 rows, and Northern Ireland, which is in the United Kingdom but not Great Britain, is missing.

### Exercise 5

Replace the code in that chunk with a bar chart of the total number of respondents giving each `opinion`, with the answers on the y-axis. Render.

```{r}
  summarize(n = sum(n), .by = opinion) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = opinion)) +
```

The plot sorts the answers alphabetically, with Don't know at the bottom and Very well at the top. The alphabetical ordering isn't particularly meaningful for describing the data.

### Exercise 6

Order the bars by the number of respondents, with the longest bar at the top. Render.

```{r}
#| label: order-labels-purpose-and-color-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: order-labels-purpose-and-color-6-test
#| echo: true
read_csv("data/brexit.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  summarize(n = sum(n), .by = opinion) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = fct_reorder(opinion, n))) +
  geom_col()
```

###

Sometimes it makes sense to order the bars from tallest to shortest (or vice versa), which makes the most common answer obvious. But this order scatters the two positive answers and the two negative ones, which belong together.

### Exercise 7

Put the bars in the order the survey offered the answers, with Very well at the top and Don't know at the bottom. Render.

```{r}
#| label: order-labels-purpose-and-color-7
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: order-labels-purpose-and-color-7-test
#| echo: true
read_csv("data/brexit.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  summarize(n = sum(n), .by = opinion) |>
  mutate(opinion = fct_relevel(opinion, "Very well", "Fairly well",
                               "Fairly badly", "Very badly", "Don't know")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = fct_rev(opinion))) +
  geom_col()
```

###

In this case, the best ordering is probably the one in which the questions were asked. An ordering which does not make sense in the context of the problem (e.g., alphabetically here), can mislead the reader who might take a quick glance at the axes and not read the bar labels carefully.

### Exercise 8

Replace the code in that chunk so that it only reads `data/brexit.csv` and stores it as `brexit`, with `opinion` in the survey's order and `region` ordered from south to north: London, Rest of South, Midlands / Wales, North, and Scotland. Render.

```{r}
#| label: order-labels-purpose-and-color-8
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: order-labels-purpose-and-color-8-test
#| echo: true
brexit <- read_csv("data/brexit.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(opinion = fct_relevel(opinion, "Very well", "Fairly well",
                               "Fairly badly", "Very badly", "Don't know"),
         region = fct_relevel(region, "London", "Rest of South",
                              "Midlands / Wales", "North", "Scotland"))
```

###

A categorical variable stored with its levels in a fixed order carries that order into every later table and plot. Most software programs have built in methods for some of the plot details -- some order levels alphabetically, some provide functionality for arranging them in a custom order.

### Exercise 12

Replace the code in that chunk with a separate bar chart of the number of respondents giving each `opinion` for each `region`, side by side, with the answers on the y-axis in the survey's order. Use few enough tick marks that the numbers on the x-axes do not run together. Render.

```{r}
#| label: order-labels-purpose-and-color-12
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: order-labels-purpose-and-color-12-test
#| echo: true
brexit |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = fct_rev(opinion))) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ region, nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 100, 200))
```

###

Splitting one plot into a panel for each group is called faceting, and it shows the shape of opinion within each region. Depending on your research question, stacked bar plots may not tell the part of the story most important to the research.

```{r}
#| label: order-labels-purpose-and-color-13-test
#| echo: true
brexit |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = region, fill = opinion)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "cividis")
```

###

Default or rainbow colors are not always the choice which will best distinguish the level of your variables. The cividis scale works well with ordinal data, and it was designed by Nuñez and colleagues to look the same to people with and without color vision deficiency.

Improve the plot. Put Very well at the left end of each bar, show the x-axis as percentages, and put the legend on top. Use the survey question as the title, and add a subtitle that states the main finding and a caption giving the number of respondents and the source. Remove the axis titles. Render.

```{r}
#| label: order-labels-purpose-and-color-14

```

###

```{r}
#| label: order-labels-purpose-and-color-14-test
#| echo: true
brexit |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = region, fill = opinion)) +
  geom_col(position = position_fill(reverse = TRUE)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "cividis") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(title = "How well or badly do you think the government are doing\nat handling Britain's exit from the European Union?",
       subtitle = "Very badly was the top answer in every region, from 43% in Midlands / Wales to 63% in Scotland",
       x = NULL,
       y = NULL,
       fill = NULL,
       caption = "1,643 Great Britain adults; YouGov, 2-3 September 2019") +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        plot.title.position = "plot")
```

###

Labels should be clear and oriented horizontally for the reader. Don't forget titles and, if possible, include the source of the data.

The fundamental principle is that your graph should provide maximal information succinctly and clearly. Order, orientation, proportion, and color each changed what the same 25 numbers said.

## Summary

This tutorial covered [Chapter 6: Applications: Explore](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/explore-applications.html) from [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. You have learned the chapter's principles for communicating exploratory results: keep it simple, use color to draw attention, tell a story, put categories in a meaningful order, make labels easy to read, pick a purpose, and select meaningful colors.

For the research behind the cividis scale, read "[Optimizing colormaps with consideration for color vision deficiency to enable accurate interpretation of scientific data](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0199239)" by Nuñez, Anderton, and Renslow, which the chapter cites. For the poll itself, see YouGov's [survey results](https://d25d2506sfb94s.cloudfront.net/cumulus_uploads/document/x0msmggx08/YouGov%20-%20Brexit%20and%202019%20election.pdf).

Many sentences in this tutorial come from the chapter, used under the book's [CC BY-SA 3.0 license](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/).
